sections.heading: Unregistered Validator Exits and Withdrawal Delay
sections.summary: Unregistered validators will be immediately exited at the PQ fork with a 16,384-epoch (~72 day) withdrawal delay; no changes made.
sections.body:
- Since the previous call, the spec was updated so that validators without PQ key material are immediately exited at the fork (rather than merely having their exit initiated), but with a very long withdrawal delay of 16,384 epochs (~72 days) to allow time for potential social slashing.
- Lighthouse (ethDreamer) questioned whether social slashing is realistic: once the PQ transition is finalized, old BLS keys cannot do much beyond long-range attacks. Keeping funds locked for 72 days may be unnecessarily harsh.
- Francesco clarified that the bigger safety concern is not the exited validators' keys but the reduction in quorum size when they leave the active set. This is an inherent trade-off: keeping them in the set preserves safety but hurts liveness, while exiting them does the opposite.
  - The mitigation is to not fork until a high percentage (e.g., 80–90%) of validators have registered PQ keys, so the exiting set is small.
- For validators that do hold both BLS and PQ keys, automatic cross-fork slashing is not planned; manual/social slashing may still be needed.
- Barnabas objected to relying on social slashing, saying issues should be solved in-protocol.
- No changes were made to the 16,384-epoch withdrawal delay; the group moved on.

sections.heading: Attestation Committee Reduction and Aggregator Selection
sections.summary: Committees reduced from 64 to 16 (matching subnets); aggregators are now 4 per committee, selected by effective-balance-weighted RANDAO sampling.
sections.body:
- MAX_COMMITTEES_PER_SLOT was reduced from 64 to 16, mirroring the earlier reduction of ATTESTATION_SUBNET_COUNT from 64 to 16, restoring a 1:1 committee-to-subnet mapping.
- MAX_VALIDATORS_PER_COMMITTEE will be 4× its current value to accommodate potential growth toward 1 million validators; Justin Traglia to make this change.
- Aggregator selection was changed from VRF self-selection to deterministic RANDAO-based sampling weighted by effective balance. Each committee now has exactly 4 assigned aggregators stored in a new `aggregation_committee_window` field in the beacon state, analogous to the proposer lookahead.
  - Prysm (Potuz) confirmed this is acceptable as long as a stable lookahead exists in the state.
- Whether PQDC would also use 16 committees was raised; Mikhail said it is likely, as the constraint is PQ-related rather than consensus-algorithm-related.

sections.heading: Best-Aggregate Propagation Rule
sections.summary: The "best aggregate" gossip rule was discussed but ultimately will be reverted; Potuz proposed staggered aggregator sending as an alternative.
sections.body:
- Justin Traglia introduced a spec change where only the "best" aggregate per committee (highest total effective balance of included attestations) would be propagated on the `beacon_aggregate_and_proof` topic, reducing traffic to ~16 aggregates per slot.
- Mikhail raised concerns: a malicious or early aggregate with slightly more than half the bits set could suppress all subsequent legitimate aggregates from the same subnet.
- Potuz noted that this rule guarantees some attestations will be excluded from the next slot's block, forcing the next proposer to perform expensive recursion.
- The group agreed the rule has censorship and robustness drawbacks; similar proposals have been discussed for years without adoption.
- Potuz proposed an alternative: order the 4 aggregators deterministically, stagger their send times (e.g., 500 ms apart), and have later aggregators self-censor if their aggregate is not substantially better than what they have already seen.
  - This reduces bandwidth without network-level enforcement of "best."
- Decision: Justin Traglia will revert the best-aggregate changes and fall back to the existing superset rule; the staggered-sending idea will be explored later.

sections.heading: Aggregation Performance Benchmarks
sections.summary: LeanVM 16-to-1 recursion takes ~5 seconds on 4 threads (NUC-class hardware); optimizations and reproducible benchmarks are planned for the next day.
sections.body:
- Potuz reported that his NUC (solo-staker-class, ~$1,200 US) takes ~5 seconds for a 16-to-1 STARK recursion on 4 threads; a cloud VPS used by another contributor measured ~15 seconds.
  - XMSS signature aggregation (first level, not recursion) was ~2 seconds for ~1,400 signatures on the same NUC (Potuz initially mis-stated it as under 1 second and corrected himself).
- Kamil reported 5 seconds for 16-to-1 on his VPS as well.
- Tom (LeanVM) noted that signing is intentionally unoptimized and that multi-buffer SIMD and Merkle-tree pre-caching could significantly reduce times; he committed to benchmarking with concurrent EL block execution on the same hardware by the next day.
  - Target: bring recursion closer to 2–3 seconds.
- Mikhail's napkin math: with 16 subnets and ~30,000 validators per slot, subnet-level aggregation alone takes ~5 seconds, leaving only ~4 seconds for attestation and aggregate propagation—tight for the current 9-second window.
  - 2 aggregators per subnet produce ~7 MB of aggregates plus ~2 MB of raw attestations; with gossipsub amplification factor ~8×, this implies >100 Mbit/s bandwidth.
- Kevaundray urged reproducible benchmarks: run with a fixed thread count (e.g., 4 threads) on idle hardware, then separately measure degradation when EL duties run on the remaining cores.
  - Potuz declined to stop his live validator; Justin Traglia volunteered to re-run benchmarks with the validator turned off.
  - On Justin's validator with 8 threads, standard deviation was ±29.8%; on Potuz's NUC with 8 threads it was ±5%.
- Proof sizes: subnet-level aggregate proof is ~200–210 KB (rate 1/4 Reed-Solomon); after 16-to-1 recursion, the proof is ~300 KB (rate 1/2).

sections.heading: Delayed Attestation Inclusion
sections.summary: Agreement to delay on-chain attestation inclusion to N+2 slots, removing LeanVM recursion from the critical path and simplifying the proposer's job.
sections.body:
- Potuz proposed that proposers include attestations from two slots ago (N+2) instead of the previous slot (N+1), decoupling the recursion computation from the block-production deadline.
  - With delayed inclusion, the 5-second recursion time is no longer a blocker: aggregation can begin at second 0 of the slot using attestations already in hand.
- Trade-off: in borderline-finalization scenarios, finality could be delayed by one slot. The group considered this acceptable; the `MIN_ATTESTATION_INCLUSION_DELAY` can be increased.
- Mikhail noted that even if a proposer cannot complete aggregation for its own slot, a later "powerful" proposer can catch up and include the backlog.
- Potuz flagged secondary concerns: trustless builder payments and `get_proposer_head` logic may need adjustment when same-slot attestations are unavailable.
- Mikhail clarified that even with delayed inclusion, subnet-level XMSS aggregation (via LeanVM) is still on the hot path—it cannot be removed unless all aggregation is deferred.
- No objections: the group agreed to proceed with delayed inclusion in the spec.

sections.heading: PQ Gasper vs. PQ Decoupled Consensus
sections.summary: The group will continue developing the PQ Gasper spec and prototype first; if aggregation propagation proves infeasible, the fallback is PQDC.
sections.body:
- Potuz asked how PQDC concretely solves the aggregate propagation problem; Mikhail explained that in DC, the head-vote committee is only ~500 validators (no aggregation needed for fork choice), while heavier finality-vote aggregation happens off the critical path with more time.
  - Francesco listed DC advantages: votes start propagating from t=0 s instead of t=3 s; aggregation computation can be pipelined with broadcasting; latency is non-critical so the gossipsub duplication factor can be removed.
- Potuz acknowledged DC would likely be better but argued the propagation problem partially carries over: the same average throughput of aggregates is needed to maintain a given finality time.
- Justin Traglia took a temperature check on whether to focus on PQ Gasper or pivot immediately to PQDC.
  - Consensus: continue with PQ Gasper—solving its constraints is a useful exercise, and any solution transfers to PQDC. If too many P2P changes pile up, the group will pivot to DC.
- Terence shared a [diff of DC on top of the PQ branch](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/compare/pq...pq-dc) with open questions on head-vote proof aggregation, finality-vote schemes, and builder payments.
- Francesco shared the [Goldilocks LaTeX spec](https://github.com/ethlabs-org/eth-consensus-lean/blob/main/specs/goldilocks/tex/goldilocks-spec.tex) as final.

sections.heading: Networking Methodology and Simulation vs. Devnet Debate
sections.summary: Csaba and Kamil will document a methodology combining simulations (for scaling) and smaller devnets (for implementation realism) to answer networking questions.
sections.body:
- Kevaundray asked for a clear methodology for answering networking questions (e.g., 2 KB vs. 4 KB signature sizes): simulations, large devnets, or both?
- Kamil described his approach: a PQ gateway in front of a Prysm node that inflates BLS signatures to XMSS size, combined with bandwidth profiling and simulations (up to 13K nodes on a 500 GB machine). He shared his simulation tool: https://kamilsa.github.io/leansim/
- Csaba argued that large-scale devnets (e.g., 10,000 nodes) are expensive and not more informative than simulations for scaling properties, since scaling is mathematically predictable. Devnets are valuable for testing implementation-level interactions (EL/CL cross-traffic, real code paths) but not for exploring parameter space.
  - Both simulations and smaller devnets are needed, but for different purposes.
- Mikhail countered that realistic PQ devnets must account for EL bandwidth, CPU load, and PQ mempool behavior—hard to capture in pure simulation.
- Potuz noted previous 1,000-node devnets for RLNC were expensive and short-lived.
- Action item: Csaba (lead) and Kamil will produce a written methodology document explaining what simulations cover, what devnets cover, and the rationale for not needing massive-scale devnets.
- Action item: Kamil will continue running simulations, including measuring gains from large-message broadcast optimizations for proofs.
- Historical mainnet data (via Xatu/Panda) was identified as useful for calibrating bandwidth assumptions under PQ signature sizes.

sections.heading: Devnet-0 Planning and Action Items
sections.summary: PQ-devnet-0 will genesis directly at PQ (no BLS keys, no fork transition); spec commit expected within hours, client prototyping to begin immediately.
sections.body:
- Agreement to genesis at PQ rather than testing the fork transition, since the goal is feasibility testing of PQ aggregation, not transition logic.
  - No BLS keys at all in the genesis state; deposit requests and BLS-related execution requests will be removed/commented out for the devnet.
  - Potuz confirmed no deposit contract is needed; genesis will use a static validator set.
- Justin Traglia committed to having the spec (with delayed inclusion changes) ready for implementation within ~3 hours; a commit will be shared on the PQCL Discord channel.
- Key generation: LeanVM supports XMSS key generation via Rust bindings. Pub-key generation is fast; signing 21,000 signatures took minutes on Potuz's machine (but this is not needed at genesis).
- Barnabas volunteered to work on Kurtosis tooling for PQ genesis, using `pq-devnet-0` as the branch name. Pre-generated validator keys may be pushed to an S3 bucket to avoid per-node generation delays.
- Terence urged async coordination on Discord to avoid duplicated effort on tooling.
- Kevaundray summarized action items:
  1. Finish the spec with delayed aggregator inclusion (Justin Traglia)
  2. Clients will vibe-code implementations matching the spec
  3. Networking team will run simulations for confidence
  4. Networking folks will document methodology for answering networking questions

sections.heading: 0x02 Validator Restriction for PQ Registration
sections.summary: Restricting PQ key registration to 0x02 validators was broadly supported; this encourages consolidation but is not needed for the first devnet.
sections.body:
- Francesco proposed requiring validators to have 0x02 withdrawal credentials before they can register PQ key material, arguing that the main barrier to consolidation is touching the withdrawal credential at all—once required, there is little reason not to consolidate.
  - 0x02 validators already represent ~20M ETH; Lido's consolidation will soon bring this to ~25M, reducing the validator count toward ~600K.
- Barnabas suggested measuring PQ registration readiness against the 0x02 subset only (e.g., 2/3 of 0x02 validators), rather than the full validator set.
- Justin Traglia expressed mild concern that this could delay PQ registrations but was overall supportive.
- Kevaundray noted this may require including EIP-8148 (custom sweep threshold for validators) in the H-star fork; Barnabas confirmed 8148 is already CFI.
- Mikhail raised a gatekeeping risk: large entities could delay PQ registration to block the fork. Francesco countered that such entities could simply be exited at the fork.
- Decision: the restriction is supported in principle but will not be included in the first devnet prototype; Terence's existing code omits it.

sections.heading: Call Cadence and Logistics
sections.summary: The group will likely reduce to two PQCL breakout calls per week; final decision deferred to Friday's call.
sections.body:
- Three 2-hour calls per week was deemed excessive by multiple participants; Francesco and Potuz both advocated for one call per week, or at most two.
- The Tuesday PQCL slot conflicts with the Frames breakout call; if a call is dropped, it should be Tuesday's.
- Decision deferred to Friday's call; the group will evaluate whether the current pace of progress justifies the meeting frequency.
- The current devnet prototype is built on top of Glamsterdam, not Heze; the PQ fork itself is envisioned as part of H-star.
